subtype: Teen living in a dim room [Actor]
passage:
Since the exams ended, Kavitha had lived in the back room of their house in Palakkad with the wooden shutters closed. She slept till eleven, lay under a sheet with her phone, and couldn't say whether it was Wednesday or Friday. She felt heavy, like the air in the room.
One morning her little brother Dhruv flung the shutters open. "Amma says breakfast is on the verandah. Now." Sunlight fell across the bed. Kavitha groaned, but went.
The verandah smelled of wet earth. Paati was stringing jasmine. Kavitha sat beside her and helped, blinking in the light.
The next morning she woke at seven and opened the shutters herself. By the end of the week she was walking to the temple tank with Paati before breakfast, and the heaviness had begun to lift.

qa.q: What was Paati stringing?
qa.a: Paati was stringing jasmine.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel living with the shutters closed?
qa.a: Kavitha felt heavy and flat, and lost track of the days.

qa.q: What helped Kavitha's mood begin to lift?
qa.a: Morning sunlight, breakfast on the verandah, and a set early walk to the temple tank with Paati.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see his sister's shuttered room?
qa.a: Dhruv seems to see it as a dark place Kavitha needed pulling out of, so he flung the shutters open.

grounding: A teenager's mood drops in a shuttered room, and morning light and an early rhythm gently lift her energy.

subtype: Teen living in a dim room [Actor]
passage: After the board exams ended, Jyoti drew the heavy curtains in her room in their Kolkata flat and more or less stayed there. She slept at four, woke at one, ate in front of her laptop. The days blurred. By the third week she couldn't remember if it was Tuesday or Saturday, and she felt flat and teary for no reason. Her friend Ayesha came over and wrinkled her nose. 'It's like a cave in here.' She yanked the curtains open. Jyoti squinted at the flood of light. 'Tomorrow, eight o'clock, terrace. We're having chai in the sun. I'll call you.' Ayesha called at eight. Jyoti grumbled, but went up. They did it every morning that week. By Sunday, Jyoti was sleeping by midnight and actually wanted to go out.

qa.q: What time did Ayesha call?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: How was Jyoti feeling by the third week?
qa.a: She felt flat and teary for no reason, with the days blurring together.

qa.q: What did Ayesha's plan change for Jyoti?
qa.a: Morning sunlight on the terrace and a set wake time gently reset Jyoti's sleep and lifted her energy.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt walking into the dark room?
qa.a: Ayesha was probably surprised and concerned to find her friend living in a cave.

subtype: Teen living in a dim room [Actor]
passage:
'Manoj, it's one o'clock.' Leela pulled back the curtains. Light poured across the unmade bed.
'Mumma! Close them!'
'You've had them shut for two weeks. You said yourself you feel like a zombie.'
'Because there's nothing to do in the holidays.'
'Or because you haven't seen daylight since Diwali.' Leela sat on the bed. 'You're grumpy, you're tired even after twelve hours, and yesterday you didn't know what day it was.'
Manoj said nothing.
'Deal. You get up at eight. We have chai on the balcony together, in the sun. Then do what you like.'
'Eight is so early.'
'Try it for a week.'
Four days later, Manoj was waiting on the balcony with two cups. 'Weird,' he said, squinting at the sun. 'I actually feel awake.'

qa.q: What time was it when Leela pulled back the curtains?
qa.a: One o'clock.

qa.q: How was Manoj feeling after two weeks in the dark room?
qa.a: He felt like a zombie, grumpy and tired even after long sleep.

qa.q: What deal did Leela offer, and why might it help?
qa.a: Getting up at eight for chai on the sunny balcony, which gives morning light and a fixed wake time.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt seeing Manoj waiting with two cups?
qa.a: She was probably pleased and relieved that the deal was working.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose mood and energy drop in a dark room, and how morning light and a set wake time lift them.

subtype: Teen living in a dim room [Actor]
passage: The summer I was fifteen, I lived in my room. Curtains shut, lights off, screen on. I told everyone I was resting after exams. Really, I felt heavy and sad in a way I couldn't explain, and every day was the same grey smear. I'm Nikita, and I didn't notice how dark it was till my cousin Swati visited from Nashik. She walked in and said, 'Nikita, it smells of old socks and sadness in here.' Then she opened the window. She made me promise to get up at seven with her while she stayed. We walked to the lake every morning, blinking in the light. By the end of her visit I was waking up by myself. I kept the curtains open after she left, and the heaviness slowly lifted.

qa.q: Where did Swati visit from?
qa.a: From Nashik.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel during the summer in the dark room?
qa.a: Nikita felt heavy and sad, with every day the same grey smear.

qa.q: What did Swati do that helped?
qa.a: Swati opened the window and set a seven o'clock wake-up with walks to the lake in morning light.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt on walking into the room?
qa.a: Swati was probably surprised and worried, and chose to use humour to lighten it.

subtype: Teen living in a dim room [Actor]
passage:
Kept for Gopika's doctor visit next week. Neelam, her mother.
Since exams ended, Gopika has kept her curtains shut. I have found her at two in the afternoon under the blanket with the phone glowing, saying she "can't tell if it's Tuesday or Friday". She stopped coming out for dinner and snapped when I switched on the tube light. I didn't pull the curtains open myself. On Saturday I asked if we could try one thing together: up at eight, tea on the balcony in the morning sun, even for ten minutes. She agreed, sulking. It is day five now. She comes out on her own carrying two cups, and yesterday she laughed at the pigeons. She still looks low some evenings, so we will mention it to the doctor.

qa.q: Where do Gopika and her mother have tea in the morning?
qa.a: They have tea on the balcony in the morning sun.

qa.q: What does Gopika's remark about not knowing the day suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels lost and low, as if her days have blurred together in the dark room.

qa.q: What did Neelam's approach get right, and what is the sensible next step?
qa.a: She offered a shared morning routine instead of forcing the curtains open, and she plans to mention the low evenings to the doctor.

qa.q: How is Neelam affected when Gopika snaps about the light?
qa.a: Neelam is hurt and worried, but chooses patience over a fight, which keeps Gopika willing to try.
